power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p < 0.2 ", "p < 0.2 "), Sentence = c("Variables with p < 0.2 in the univariable analysis were entered into the multivariable model, and results were reported as crude (cOR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).", "Variables with p < 0.2 in univariable analysis were entered into the multivariable model; blank aOR cells indicate variables not entered." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: About 0.07% to 8% of parturients will require intensive care unit (ICU) admission during pregnancy, childbirth or puerperium, with great regional variations.
When this occurs, it increases morbidity, mortality, long-term physical and psychological sequelae as well as cost.

This study sought to examine a five-year admission rate, indications and outcomes of parturients with severe morbidities admitted in the ICU at a tertiary referral facility and teaching hospital in Tanzania.

Methodology: A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar es Salaam city that included all women who were admitted to the obstetric ICU between 2019 and 2023.
Data were retrospectively collected using a pre-tested checklist from all 1526 obstetric ICU admissions, out of 29391 obstetric unit admissions, during the study period.
Sources of data were both case files and electronic registries in the ICU and labour ward.

Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with maternal mortality, with results presented as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) while indications of ICU admission and maternal outcomes were presented descriptively by using frequencies and tables.
Results: Out of 29391 obstetric unit admissions, 1526 required ICU, resulting into obstetric ICU admission rate of 5.2%.
Hypertensive disorders were the leading cause of admission (73.7%) followed by obstetric haemorrhages (15%).
Frequent ICU interventions included; mechanical ventilation (50%), anticonvulsants (26%), blood transfusion (15%), inotropes (4.2%), and dialysis (3.5%).
Maternal fatality rate was 14%.
In multivariable regression analysis, vaginal delivery was associated with 47% higher odds of mortality compared to caesarean section (aOR 1.47, 95% CI 1.03-2.11, p=0.036).
A moderate ICU stay of 3-4 days showed a 91% protective effect relative to stays of ≤2 days (aOR 0.09, P < 0.001). 5-7day stays were also protective (aOR 0.32, p=0.006).

text.text: This five years review of obstetric ICU admissions (2019obstetric ICU admissions ( -2023) )  showed that, approximately one in 20 obstetric patients required critical care, with one in seven of ICU admissions resulting in maternal death.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy accounted for majority of ICU admissions, and deaths occurred predominantly during the early phase of critical care.

These findings underscore the need to strengthen antenatal risk identification, optimise referral and emergency obstetric care, ensure timely magnesium sulphate administration, and establish obstetric high dependency units to facilitate earlier interventions.
Such measures could reduce the burden on ICUs while improving maternal outcomes.

Majority of pregnancies end uneventfully with a healthy mother and newborn, a few however may end up with unintended outcomes, caused by physiologic and anatomic changes that occur during pregnancy that put stress on different body organ systems limiting their ability to compensate during stressful conditions.
These changes heighten risk of complications involving multiple organ systems during pregnancy, labour, delivery, and after delivery [1].

Nevertheless, these differences call for local studies to understand the reasons for ICU admission in our setting to design and implement interventions based on the local context.

text.text: This study aimed to examine the rate of obstetric ICU admission, indications, and maternal outcomes, as well as the associated factors at a tertiary referral and a teaching hospital in Tanzania to provide evidence for informing practice and guiding policy change in obstetric critical care.

A five-year retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at Muhimbili National Hospital (MNH) from 1 st January 2019 to 31 st December 2023, assessing the rate of admission, indications, and outcomes of parturients with severe morbidities admitted to the obstetric critical care unit.

MNH is the largest public referral facility in Tanzania, providing tertiary care services in Dar es Salaam city serving over 5.4 million residents (Census 2022) and other referral patients residing in nearby regions.
The hospital has over 1500 bed capacity and five specialised ICUs (obstetric, medical, surgical, paediatrics, and neonatal), all adequately equipped to provide critical care services.
The obstetric ICU has 15 beds all equipped with mechanical ventilators.
It is an open ICU, run by a dedicated team of obstetricians, intensivists, anaesthesiologists, nurses and other allied healthcare providers.
Rarely, when adult ICUs are full, female patients may be admitted into the obstetric ICU without obstetric indications.
During the study period, there were 1526 admissions to the obstetric critical care, 66 of them were not due to obstetric reasons.
The hospital has 18 operating rooms, of which four are dedicated for obstetric and gynaecological surgeries.
There are 15 delivery beds in the labour suit where all vaginal births are conducted, except a few sick mothers that deliver in the obstetric ICU.
Following obstetric ICU and labour ward admissions, all patients' information are documented in the registry books and electronically.
Recorded data include name, age, registration number, parity, diagnosis (indication of admission), mode and date of delivery, as well as foetal and maternal outcomes and their dispositions.
There were a total of 1526 obstetric ICU admissions between January 2019 and December 2023.
A consecutive (census) sampling approach was used.
All obstetric ICU admissions from1 st January 2019 to 31 st December 2023 were consecutively assessed for eligibility for inclusion.
Inclusion criterion was patients who were admitted to the obstetric ICU, while patients with missing information of interest or admitted with non-obstetric reasons were excluded.
A pre-tested checklist was used to extract data from June to December 2024.

Research assistants were responsible for data extraction under supervision from the principal investigator who had access to the all-relevant registries that could identify participants during the period of the study but not after.
Variables of interest included socio-demographics and obstetric characteristics, indication of ICU admission, date and mode of delivery as well as foetal and maternal outcomes and their disposition.

Of the 1526 obstetric ICU admissions, 211 patients had missing information from either torn pages or incomplete documentation while 66 were admitted with non-obstetric conditions, and therefore excluded.
Data of 1249 admissions who met inclusion criteria were analysed using an SPSS ver.
20 (Chicago, Illinois, USA).
Descriptive summary of frequencies, percentages and tables, were applied to present the rate of ICU admission, indications of admission, foetal, and maternal outcomes.
Univariable and multivariable logistic regression were applied to analyse factors associated with maternal outcomes.

Variables with p < 0.2 in the univariable analysis were entered into the multivariable model, and results were reported as crude (cOR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

This study examined the frequency, indications, and maternal outcomes of obstetric ICU admissions, and the factors associated with mortality, at a tertiary referral and teaching hospital in Tanzania.
About one in 20 obstetric admissions required intensive care, with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy accounting for nearly three-quarters of these, followed by obstetric haemorrhage.
Approximately one in seven women admitted to the ICU died.
Vaginal delivery was associated with higher odds of mortality compared to caesarean section, whereas receipt of anticonvulsant therapy was independently associated with a reduced risk of death.

In addition, an ICU stay of three to four days was associated with lower odds of mortality compared with a stay of two days or less, suggesting that the highest mortality occurred during the early phase of critical illness.
The obstetric ICU admission rate of 5.2% in the present study is high and consistent with the marked global disparities previously reported in critical care admission following delivery.

For example, an observational study in China reported a peripartum ICU admission rate of about 1% [26], considerably lower than our finding and those from other sub-Saharan African settings [22, 27, 28].
text.formatted: For example, an observational study in China reported a peripartum ICU admission rate of about 1% <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>, considerably lower than our finding and those from other sub-Saharan African settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: However, most of these were single-centre observational studies that used different denominators (deliveries, obstetric admissions or all ICU admissions), which limit direct comparison.
At the regional level, a systematic review and meta-analysis from Africa found that obstetric patients accounted for about 17% of all ICU admissions [29].
text.formatted: At the regional level, a systematic review and meta-analysis from Africa found that obstetric patients accounted for about 17% of all ICU admissions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: These disparities likely reflect regional differences in health-system infrastructure, severity of illness at presentation, and access to timely intervention.

In low-resource settings, the three delays (in deciding to seek care, reaching a facility, and receiving adequate treatment) have consistently been linked to the escalation of obstetric complications into critical illness [28, 29].
text.formatted: In low-resource settings, the three delays (in deciding to seek care, reaching a facility, and receiving adequate treatment) have consistently been linked to the escalation of obstetric complications into critical illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: As MNH is a tertiary referral hospital, delays at any of these levels may have contributed to its high ICU admission rate.
Structural constraints may also contribute.

Studies from the African region show that, in the absence of step-down facilities such as HDUs, health facilities often admit even patients who require only observation and monitoring to the ICU, inflating ICU admission rates [27, 29].
text.formatted: Studies from the African region show that, in the absence of step-down facilities such as HDUs, health facilities often admit even patients who require only observation and monitoring to the ICU, inflating ICU admission rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: This is supported by evidence from China, where the introduction of an obstetric HDU substantially reduced ICU admissions [26].

text.text: Because MNH had no obstetric HDU during the study period, the lack of this intermediate level of care may partly explain the high ICU admission rate observed.
In the present study, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were the leading indication for ICU admission (73.7%), followed by severe obstetric haemorrhage (15.0%).
This pattern is consistent with earlier findings at MNH [21] and with reports from other settings in Africa and Asia [4, [7] [8] [9] 13, 14].

text.text: Although the indications for obstetric ICU admission are broadly similar in highincome countries (HICs) and low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), hypertensive disorders account for a far higher proportion of admissions in LMICs (43-70%) than in HICs [27, 29, 30].

text.text: In HICs, a growing share of admissions is due to indirect obstetric causes such as cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension and complications of assisted reproduction [31, 32], reflecting older maternal age and more comorbidities.

text.text: Because hypertensive disorders are largely detectable through routine antenatal screening, their predominance in our cohort suggests gaps in antenatal care (ANC), particularly in early screening, detection and optimisation of medical conditions, and timely referral for specialised care.
This is supported by a recent analysis of Tanzanian national survey data, which found that nearly half of pregnant women had an inadequate number of ANC visits [33].

text.text: Similarly, at a Nigerian teaching hospital, about 70% of women admitted to the obstetric ICU had not booked for ANC [28].

text.text: Strengthening ANC to ensure early detection and optimisation of maternal medical conditions, with timely referral, is therefore essential [34].

text.text: The maternal ICU mortality of 14% in our study is high and consistent with a systematic review and meta-analysis from the African region [29] and with observational studies from other lowresource settings in Africa and Asia [19, 28, 35].

text.text: In contrast, studies from some European countries have reported obstetric ICU mortality as low as 2% [18].

text.text: Consistent with this, a systematic review found obstetric ICU mortality to be nine times higher in LMICs than in HICs [36].

text.text: These marked regional differences in maternal ICU mortality highlight an opportunity for improving maternal critical care outcomes in LMICs, given that about 50% of maternal deaths are considered avoidable [14, 37].

In the multivariable analysis of factors associated with maternal ICU outcomes, only three variables remained statistically significant after adjustment for confounders.

An ICU stay of three to seven days was significantly associated with survival compared with a stay of two days or less, likely reflecting late presentation and rapid clinical deterioration before adequate treatment could be initiated.
A similar study in Asia reported a mean ICU stay of 5 days and linked stays of one day to mortality, attributing this to late referral and poor ANC; 60% of its participants had not attended ANC [39].

text.text: This study has several strengths.
It aligns with local and global efforts towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by identifying measures to reduce maternal mortality, particularly among critically ill women in the ICU.

It also highlights important outcomes of obstetric ICU admission, providing a basis for planned future projects and for practice and policy changes aimed at improving early recognition of warning signs, timely referral for specialised care, and prompt management of critically ill mothers.
This study also has some limitations.
First, 211 patients were excluded because key variables were missing or incomplete, owing to torn registry pages and incomplete documentation.
Nevertheless, the five-year study period allowed an adequate sample size to be obtained.
In addition, patient records are now stored electronically, which should improve data quality for future studies.

Second, the retrospective design made the study dependent on the accuracy and completeness of routine records; however, multiple data sources were used to reduce misclassification of indications and outcomes arising from inconsistent documentation.
Like other retrospective data, these records were also prone to bias and confounding.
However, the use of multiple clinical registries and data sources (registry books and electronic records) improved completeness and reduced selection bias.
In addition, multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for confounders.
Third, this was a singlecentre study conducted at the country's highest-level referral facility, which serves a high-risk population, and may therefore not be representative of other facilities.
However, our findings may be applicable to other tertiary referral facilities, depending on their institutional protocols and local resource constraints.
Finally, because of the cross-sectional design, only associations could be described; causation could not be established.
This study found that approximately one in twenty obstetric admissions required intensive care (5.2%), with an obstetric ICU mortality rate of 14%.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were the leading indication for ICU admission, followed by obstetric haemorrhage.
Caesarean delivery, anticonvulsant therapy, and an ICU stay of three to seven days (compared with two days or less) were independently associated with lower odds of maternal death.

The predominance of largely preventable hypertensive complications, together with the concentration of deaths within the first two days of ICU admission, highlight gaps in antenatal risk identification, timely recognition of clinical deterioration, referral pathways, and emergency obstetric management.

Strengthening antenatal screening for hypertensive disorders, ensuring timely administration of magnesium sulphate, improving referral systems, and establishing an obstetric high dependency unit could reduce the need for intensive care and improve maternal survival.

Prospective multicentre studies are warranted to identify the modifiable determinants of early ICU mortality and to evaluate interventions aimed at improving outcomes among critically ill obstetric patients.
